newsitem.title: UK: Labour seen winning UK election with big majority.
newsitem.headline: Labour seen winning UK election with big majority.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party stands to win a 43-seat majority in the coming general election, with economic issues concerning voters most, a Reuters survey published on Wednesday showed.
Nineteen out of 20 voting experts interviewed by Reuters predicted a Labour victory.
The average result of their forecasts for Labour's majority in terms of seats rose to 43 from 36 a month ago, the highest margin since the survey began last September.
Only one forecaster -- David Carlton of Warwick University -- maintained his belief in a nine-seat Conservative victory.
Around half of the panel of voting behaviour experts, who gave their forecasts on January 6 and 7, revised up their forecasts for a Labour majority. Britain's general election must be held by May 22.
Reuters has created the most comprehensive panel of experts in British voting patterns for the survey, which will be updated each month until the election.
The panellists said that despite the political debate raging over Britain's relationship with the European Union, the issue had not taken centre stage with voters.

"Europe is beginning to rise on the agenda. But it's not in the same league as the "four horsemen' of public concern. These are the National Health Service, education, law and order and unemployment," said panellist Bob Worcester, chairman of polling organisation MORI.

Conservative in-fighting over European economic and monetary union had not helped the government's image but most of the panellists said such constitutional issues tended not to make an impression during general elections.
"There won't be a sufficient difference between the two parties on (Europe) and they are both committed to a referendum," said Neil Carter, reader in politics at the University of York.

According to the rounded average of the 19 predictions for a Labour win, the ruling Conservatives are now expected to win 260 seats, compared with 262 in early December. Labour is expected to win 348 seats from the previous average forecast of 345.
The number of seats expected to be won by the Liberal Democrats and other parties remained unchanged at 25 and 27 respectively. The total number of seats in the new parliament will be 659.
Britain's main polling bodies have been unanimous so far in their predictions of a large majority for Labour. The latest MORI opinion poll in early December gave Labour a 21 percent lead.
Things have been getting steadily worse for the bedraggled 17-year-old Conservative government, despite signs of growing consumer confidence and a feeling of rising economic well-being, they said.
"A buoyant economy should mean that opinion polls should be moving in favour of the Tories, but they're not," said Paul Whitely, professor of politics at the University of Sheffield.
"Disunity, sleaze and perceptions of government incompetence explain the paradox of the economy doing well and a lack of government popularity," he said.
Whitely, who last month predicted a 35-seat majority for Labour, raised his forecast to 50 seats this time.
A majority of participants still expect a May election. But some have brought forward their forecasts to April.
"The government will find it difficult to last until May with a minority government," one contributor said.
Prime Minister John Major lost his wafer-thin majority in the lower House of Commons when Conservative MP John Gorst withdrew his support in parliament over a London hospital ward closure.
